facts.t: Broadside is the best angle for deer, elk, moose and bear.
Aim up the back of the near front leg, one third up the chest: both lungs, top of the heart.
Aim for both lungs, not the heart. The lungs are the biggest vital target and give the most room for error.
Quartering away is the second best angle.
Picture the far front leg. Aim on the near side at the spot that sends the bullet to it. The bullet enters behind the ribs and crosses both lungs.
Aiming at the near crease, like broadside, can clip only one lung.
Quartering toward: for experienced hunters only. Beginners wait for the animal to turn.
A light bullet can deflect off the shoulder bones of elk, deer or a big bear.
The trap: it looks "almost broadside". Test: can you see the roundness of the far shoulder? Then it is quartering.
Facing straight on: a small target between the shoulders, lots of bone, ruined meat. Hunter Ed: rarely a clean kill.
Walking straight away, the "Texas heart shot": no vitals in reach, guts and hams in the way. Never.
The near front leg is back and covers the heart and lower lungs. Wait for it to step forward: that opens the chest.
Broadside is still the angle you want. Patience turns this into a good shot in a few seconds.
Skylined on a ridge: no backstop. Hunter Ed: do not shoot at a skylined animal.
Not sure of the angle, the range or the backstop? That is a no.
Behind brush: a twig can deflect a bullet. Wait for a clear lane.
Another animal stands behind the vitals. The bullet exits. The second animal is your bullet too.

broadside.t: Deer vital zone with margin: about 20 to 25 cm (8 to 10 in).

qaway.t: Deer quartering away: aim at the off shoulder. The bullet enters behind the ribs and crosses both lungs.

any.t: Mule deer in the rut carry thick necks and shoulders. Keep the aim behind the shoulder, not in it.

broadside.t: Moose heart and lung zone: about the size of a basketball, the largest vital zone you will hunt.

any.t: The hump fools you: hunters centre on the body under the hump and hit above the lungs. Aim lower than instinct says.
Moose seldom drop. Wait a few minutes, then follow up every shot quietly.

broadside.t: Elk aim spot: up the back of the front leg, one third to one half up the chest.

qaway.t: Elk quartering away: aim for the far shoulder. Do not hit the paunch.

any.t: The bull elk shoulder blade sits farther back and is up to 6 cm (2.5 in) thick. Aim for the lungs, not the shoulder blade.

broadside.t: Bear: halfway up the body, tight behind the shoulder, once the near leg steps forward, through both lungs.
Bear vital zone: about a 20 cm (8 in) circle behind the front shoulder.

any.t: The heart sits low and the lungs reach well back. Long hair and fat make the bear look bigger than it is.
Shoulder and head shots on bears: not recommended. Heavy bone, and a dense, sloped skull.

facts.t: Both lungs: the animal runs hard, then wobbles. Deer: under 100 m. Wait 30 minutes before you follow.
Heart: bolts, often a jump or kick. Deer rarely go over 50 m. Wait 30 minutes.
The shoulder blade and upper leg bone sit over the front of the chest. A .308 bullet breaks them; an arrow does not.
The target is just behind the shoulder, not in it.
Muscle or leg hit: the animal keeps running at a normal pace, thin blood, goes far. Wait 30 to 60 minutes, then track hard.
Liver: kills, but slowly. Paunch: a slow death and a hard track.
Gut or liver hit: mark the spot, back out quietly and wait hours.
The spine runs along the top of the back, a little below the hair line. A near miss above it is a clean miss; a hit in the meat between is a wounded animal.
Under the heart is brisket and legs. A muscle hit: thin blood and a long track.
Head and neck: small targets, small margin, lost animals. Hunter Ed discourages them.
Hindquarter: no vitals in reach. A muscle hit: the animal keeps running, thin blood.
Pick a hair, not a deer. Shoot at an animal and you hit an animal somewhere.

buck.assume: Assumption: you hunt MU (Management Unit) 3-27 in Region 3, in the general open season, as an adult hunter, with the right licence, in legal hours.

mdPoint.t: A 4 point mule deer buck has at least 4 tines on ONE antler, not counting the brow tine.

tine.t: A tine (point) is at least 2.5 cm (1 in) long and longer than it is wide.

brow.t: The brow tine is the first point that sticks forward or up in the lower third of the antler.

mdSeason.t: Mule deer, MU 3-27: 4 point bucks 10 to 30 September; any buck 1 to 31 October; 4 point bucks 1 November to 10 December.

mdAntlers.t: Buck from a 4 point season: the antlers go with the species licence.

mdAntlerless.t: Antlerless mule deer in Region 3: only by LEH (Limited Entry Hunting) draw.

wtBucks.t: White tailed bucks, MU 3-27: 10 September to 10 December. The row says Bucks: no point rule.

wtAntlerless.t: Antlerless white tails, MU 3-27: 10 to 31 October. In November, either sex is youth only (under 18).

buck.t: A buck has visible bony antlers. A button buck, a male fawn with skin covered bumps, is antlerless.

wtCount.t: White tail point count: hunters count each tine about 2.5 cm (1 in) or longer, plus the beam tip. The brow tine counts here.

mdShape.t: Mule deer antlers fork, and fork again. White tails grow one main beam with single tines rising from it.

mdAge.t: Most yearling mule deer have 2 points a side. Older bucks have 4 or more plus a small eye guard (brow tine).

mdOther.t: Other Region 3 MUs open on other dates (3-15, 3-16, 3-32, 3-33 from 1 September; 3-46 from 20 September). Read your MU's row.

r2.note: Region 2 set for MUs 2-8, 2-18, 2-19 (one shared Bucks row on page 28). Facts copied from rb-region-2, local-harrison-deer and mc-black-tailed-deer-01, checked 2026-10-23.
r2.assume: Assumption: you hunt MU (Management Unit) {mu} in Region 2 with a rifle, in the general open season, as an adult hunter, with the right licence, in legal hours.

r2Bucks.t: Black tailed deer, MUs 2-8, 2-18 and 2-19: bucks 10 September to 15 December. The row says Bucks, not 4 point bucks.

r2Spike.t: So any buck with visible bony antlers is legal there in season, a spike included.

r2Bow.t: Bucks 1 to 9 September in these MUs are bow only. Not with a rifle.

r2Antlerless.t: No antlerless (doe or fawn) general season in MUs 2-8, 2-18 or 2-19. A button buck is antlerless.

r2Limit.t: Region 2 limit: 2 deer a licence year, at most 1 antlerless. A limit is not a season.

r2Wt.t: No white tailed deer season anywhere in Region 2.

btLaw.t: In law a black tailed deer is a mule deer: same 4 point definition, same mule deer species licence.

btShape.t: Black tail antlers branch like a mule deer's: each beam forks, then forks again.

btAge.t: On the south coast about 90% of yearling black tails are spikes; by 2.5 years most bucks have forks, 2 points a side.

wtFlag.t: A wide tail that flags up white points to a white tail. If you cannot be sure, do not shoot.

facts.t: Mule deer stand 90 to 95 cm at the shoulder. This scene draws them at 92 cm.
Chest depth, back to brisket: hunters use about 46 cm (18 in) for deer. Hunter lore, not a measured source.
Mil formula: metres = size in metres × 1,000 ÷ size in mils.
Unit of measure: picture a known 100 m, count how many fit. Needs the ground in view, poor past 400 m.
Halving: judge to a point halfway, then double it.
Bracketing: "more than X, less than Y", call the middle.
Laser first, reticle second, eye third. Hunters estimate badly without practice.
Range three landmarks before any deer shows. Range at least three times; two that agree are the answer.
Bright light, snow, water and clear air make things look nearer. Fog, dusk and a part showing make them look farther.
Why it matters: hold for 250 m on a deer at 300 m and the bullet lands about 20 cm low, the full height of the vital zone.
Practice game: guess a distance out loud, then range it. Log it. Within a month your guesses close to 10%.
